title: Mortgage Rates Trickle Down to 2-Week Lows
summary: Mortgage rates are primarily driven by day-to-day movement in the bond market. Bonds have been taking cues from turmoil in the stock market--especially among tech companies. With the NASDAQ on track to close at the 2nd lowest level since mid-April, it's no surprise to find bonds and rates are doing fairly well.   Today's rate movement was fairly muted with the average top-tier 30yr fixed rate only dropping 0.02%. Still, that's the best level in exactly 2 weeks.  You may be wondering: if bonds are taking cues from stocks and stocks are near their lowest levels since April, why are rates still so far above their levels from April?  The stock/bond relationship is far from the only consideration for bonds. In fact, there are many times where stocks are moving higher in price even as rates are dropping. There are other times where one side of the market is flat while the other is on the move.  Bonds care deeply about inflation, other economic data, and overall bond market issuance levels. All 3 have been pointing toward higher rates for most of the year, but those same 3 factors often help the stock market.  The present phenomenon (stock prices and rates moving in the same direction) didn't really kick into high gear until mid-October when concerns over the pace of AI infrastructure growth began weighing not only on AI-focused stocks, but also on the broader economic outlook.

title: Subservicing, Realtor tracking, Cyber Security Tools; Capital Markets; How to Evaluate AI Rollout
summary: Let’s check out the recent “mail bag.” “Rob, in the conversations that you’ve heard or read about ‘credit modernization,’ is there any consistency in answers or approaches?” No. I don’t even think that we have firm credit pricing for 2027. STRATMOR’s current blog is, “Artificial Intelligence, Lending, and Education.” Along those lines I was asked if the traditional vendor management role is enough to handle artificial intelligence. No, and I refer to some thoughts Mike Yu, CEO of Vesta, has. “Mortgage lenders evaluating artificial intelligence face a challenge that goes beyond choosing the right vendor: the real cost of adoption is the organizational effort required to change how work gets done. Lenders cannot simply plug in an AI solution and expect immediate savings, because human quality control, process adjustments, and implementation across individual tasks still consume time and resources. Lenders are effectively buying a long-term partner, not just software, making the vendor's industry knowledge, product judgment, and ability to guide decisions as important as its current capabilities.” (Today’s podcast can be found here. This week’s ‘casts are presented by Cenlar, which provides the highest level of mortgage servicing to client partners through the talent of its employees and extensive history of working with a diverse portfolio of banks, mortgage bankers, and credit unions. Today’s has an interview with keynote speaker Jim Moorhead on how mortgage leaders can adopt AI while ensuring organizational practices keep pace.)

title: Stronger Overnight. Taking Cues From Stocks
summary:
Bonds improved overnight in a move that almost perfectly traced weakness in the equities market. With no big ticket data on tap and no major market movers in play, yields bounced a bit with the stock market reversal that began around 9:30am ET, but that's already showing signs of reversing with the NASDAQ back near lows just before 10:30am ET. 
  
 The only potentially relevant econ data is buried in the 10am Consumer Confidence release. Traders don't care much about the headline confidence number, but the bond market occasionally cares about the labor differential. This measures the difference in 2 survey questions inside the confidence data: "jobs plentiful" vs "jobs hard to get." In today's release, that number jumped to its highest level in well over a year. In the short term, bonds didn't react, but if the differential continues trending higher, it would be one useful indicator that creates headwinds against lower rates.
